topic.subject: science
topic.title: Motion and time
topic.scope: speed, uniform and non-uniform motion, measuring time, distance-time graphs, simple pendulum

misconceptions.statement: Speed is the same thing as the distance an object travels.
misconceptions.why: Students often ignore the time component and only look at how far an object went to judge speed.
misconceptions.fix: Speed is the distance covered divided by the time taken; it is a rate, not just a length.

probe.question: Car A travels 10km in 1 hour. Car B travels 10km in 2 hours. Which has more speed?
probe.wrong_answer: They have the same speed because they both went 10km.

misconceptions.root_belief: confusing a rate with a quantity

misconceptions.statement: Only objects that move very fast have speed.
misconceptions.why: In everyday language, 'speed' is often used as a synonym for 'high velocity'.
misconceptions.fix: Every moving object has a speed, whether it is a crawling snail or a jet plane.

probe.question: Does a slow-moving tortoise have speed?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is too slow to have speed.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: To calculate speed, you should divide the time taken by the distance covered.
misconceptions.why: Students often memorize formulas incorrectly or assume the order of numbers in a word problem dictates the division.
misconceptions.fix: Speed is always distance divided by time (S = D/T).

probe.question: If a bus travels 100 km in 2 hours, what is its speed?

misconceptions.statement: A heavier pendulum bob will swing faster and have a shorter time period.
misconceptions.why: Intuition suggests that heavier objects fall or move faster due to gravity.
misconceptions.fix: The time period of a simple pendulum depends only on its length, not on the mass of the bob.

probe.question: If you replace a plastic bob with a metal bob of the same size, what happens to the time period?
probe.wrong_answer: The time period will decrease because the metal bob is heavier.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

misconceptions.statement: Increasing the amplitude (swing distance) of a pendulum increases its time period.
misconceptions.why: Students think that because the bob has to travel a longer distance, it must take more time.
misconceptions.fix: For small angles, the time period remains constant regardless of the amplitude.

probe.question: If you pull a pendulum back further, how does the time for one swing change?
probe.wrong_answer: It will take more time because it has further to travel.

misconceptions.root_belief: more distance always means more time

misconceptions.statement: A distance-time graph is a literal map or picture of the path taken by the object.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the visual representation of data with a physical drawing of the road or track.
misconceptions.fix: A graph shows the relationship between two variables (distance and time), not the physical shape of the route.

probe.question: If a distance-time graph is a straight line sloping upwards, is the car going up a hill?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the car is driving up a slope.

misconceptions.root_belief: a graph is a literal picture

misconceptions.statement: A steeper line on a distance-time graph means the object is moving 'higher' or 'upward'.
misconceptions.why: The visual 'upward' direction of the line is interpreted as physical height.
misconceptions.fix: A steeper slope on a distance-time graph indicates a higher speed, not a change in altitude.

probe.question: What does a very steep line on this graph tell you about the object's motion?
probe.wrong_answer: It is climbing a very steep mountain.

misconceptions.statement: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the object is moving at a constant speed.
misconceptions.why: Students often confuse 'constant speed' (straight diagonal line) with 'constant position' (horizontal line).
misconceptions.fix: A horizontal line means the distance is not changing, so the object is at rest (zero speed).

probe.question: A graph shows a flat horizontal line at 5 meters. How fast is the object moving?
probe.wrong_answer: It is moving at a steady, constant speed.

misconceptions.root_belief: straight lines always mean constant motion

misconceptions.statement: Uniform motion means the object is moving in a straight line at any speed.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the 'uniformity' of the path rather than the 'uniformity' of the speed.
misconceptions.fix: Uniform motion specifically means moving at a constant speed along a straight line.

probe.question: If a car goes around a circular track at a constant 40 km/h, is it in uniform motion?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the speed is not changing.

misconceptions.root_belief: one attribute defines the whole concept

misconceptions.statement: One oscillation is the movement from one side of the swing to the other side.
misconceptions.why: Students perceive a single 'stroke' of motion as a complete event.
misconceptions.fix: One oscillation is the complete to-and-fro motion from one point back to the same point in the same direction.

probe.question: If a bob moves from extreme left to extreme right, has it completed one oscillation?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it has finished its swing.

misconceptions.statement: The line that is physically higher on the graph always represents the faster object.
misconceptions.why: Students look at the Y-axis value (position) instead of the rate of change (slope).
misconceptions.fix: Speed is represented by the slope; a lower line can represent a faster object if it is steeper.

probe.question: Line A is at the top of the graph but flat. Line B is at the bottom but very steep. Which is faster?
probe.wrong_answer: Line A because it is higher up on the distance scale.

misconceptions.root_belief: higher position means a larger value

misconceptions.statement: You can calculate speed by dividing kilometers by minutes without any conversion.
misconceptions.why: Students ignore the standard pairing of units (km with hours, meters with seconds).
misconceptions.fix: Units must be consistent; speed is usually expressed in km/h or m/s.

probe.question: If a car travels 5 km in 10 minutes, is its speed 0.5 km/h?

problems: misconception dropped: 'A distance-time graph is a literal map or picture '
